opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the first things people find counterintuitive, so it's worth unpacking.

The intuition comes from superposition. We've known for a while that networks seem to represent more features than they have dimensions in activation space. They do this by packing features into nearly orthogonal directions and relying on the fact that most features are sparse, meaning only a few are active on any given input. If that's true of activations, there's no reason the computations acting on those activations should be limited by the number of dimensions either. A network might be implementing far more distinct mechanisms than its width, each used only on a small fraction of inputs.

So when we decompose a weight matrix into rank-one subcomponents, we aren't trying to find a basis. A basis would cap you at the matrix's rank, and you'd get something like an SVD, which is great for compression but tends to smear many mechanisms across each component. Instead we're looking for an overcomplete set of pieces that sum to the original parameters. Any single piece on its own is simple: it reads from one direction and writes to another. The key constraint is that, on any given input, only a small number of those pieces should actually matter for what the network computes.

That's what makes the overcompleteness well-posed. With an overcomplete set, there are infinitely many ways to write the matrix as a sum, so you need something to pick out the right one. In our methods, that's the requirement that you can ablate most subcomponents on a given datapoint without changing the output, together with simplicity and faithfulness. Faithfulness means the pieces have to add back up to the real weights. Simplicity means each piece should be low-rank. Minimality means as few as possible should be causally necessary on each input. Together these push you toward a decomposition where each subcomponent corresponds to something like a single mechanism.

A good way to picture it is a dictionary of computations rather than a coordinate system. A sparse autoencoder gives you an overcomplete dictionary of directions in activation space. Parameter decomposition gives you an overcomplete dictionary of little operations in weight space, most of which are switched off at any moment.

There's also a nice consistency check. In toy models where we deliberately build in more mechanisms than dimensions, like compressed computation setups where a network computes many sparse functions through a narrow layer, the decomposition recovers those mechanisms. That's evidence it's finding something real rather than an artifact of the overcomplete parameterization.

The open question is how far that holds in large models, and whether the number of subcomponents you need scales gracefully. But conceptually, if you take superposition seriously, an overcomplete decomposition of the parameters isn't strange at all. It's what you'd expect to need.

r001.rationale: The response connects superposed features in activation space to rank-one pieces that read from individual directions, allowing computations to exceed the activation width.

r002.rationale: It describes rank-one pieces as small operations and says each subcomponent corresponds to something like a single mechanism.

r003.rationale: It discusses ablation and causal necessity, but does not identify stochastic estimation as a way to determine which components matter for an input.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things that trips people up at first, because it sounds like it should be impossible. If your residual stream is, say, 512-dimensional, how can you have more than 512 meaningful rank-one pieces of a weight matrix? Isn't the matrix itself at most rank 512?

And the answer is that we're not doing a factorization in the linear-algebra sense. We're not asking for an orthogonal basis or a low-rank approximation where the pieces have to be independent of each other. We're asking a different question, which is: what is the set of mechanisms the network actually uses, and can we write the weights as a sum of those mechanisms, where each mechanism is a rank-one matrix, an outer product of an input direction and an output direction?

The thing that makes that question well-posed, even when the number of pieces exceeds the dimensionality, is sparsity in how they're used. On any given input, the network only needs a small subset of these subcomponents to produce its output. So you can have thousands of them, and they can overlap, they can be non-orthogonal, they can interfere with each other in the way superposition always does, but on any particular forward pass only a handful are doing the work. That's exactly the same picture as feature superposition in activations, where you have more features than neurons because the features are sparse. We're just moving the picture into parameter space.

So the way we make sense of it is roughly: think of the weight matrix as a kind of compressed storage for a large number of simple computations. Each computation reads a direction and writes a direction. Because the computations are rarely all active at once, you can pack more of them into the matrix than the dimensionality would naively allow, and the network tolerates the interference because it averages out or because the training distribution never asks for the colliding ones together.

Then the decomposition method, which we call Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition, is basically trying to recover that packing. You train a set of rank-one subcomponents such that, first, they sum to the original weights, so you're faithful to the model. Second, for each input, you can get the model's output using only a sparse subset of them, so they're minimal in use. And third, you want them to be as simple as possible, so you push the rank of what's active on any given datapoint down. Those constraints together are what pick out a decomposition that reflects mechanisms rather than just some arbitrary basis.

I find the right intuition is to stop thinking of the matrix as a linear map and start thinking of it as a lookup of many little maps that happen to be stored in the same place. Once you do that, having more pieces than dimensions is not paradoxical at all. It's just a statement about how much the network has compressed its computation.

r001.rationale: It connects sparse feature superposition in activations to parameter-space components and says each rank-one computation reads an input direction.

r002.rationale: It describes each rank-one component as a mechanism or simple computation that reads an input direction and writes an output direction.

r003.rationale: It does not describe stochastic estimation or causal importance as a way to identify which components matter for an input.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is between a basis and an overcomplete decomposition. If you take a matrix and do a singular value decomposition, you get a set of rank-one components whose number is bounded by the dimensions of the matrix. But that bound doesn’t mean you can’t express the matrix as a sum of more rank-one terms. It means those additional terms can’t all be independent.

Each rank-one term can be thought of as reading out one direction in the input and writing in one direction in the output. You could have many such operations whose sum gives you the original weight matrix, even if their input and output directions overlap.

The motivation is that the number of meaningful features or computations represented by a network might be much larger than the dimensionality of its activation space. That’s the idea of superposition: you can accommodate lots of features if they’re only sparsely active, without giving each one its own orthogonal direction.

But simply making the decomposition overcomplete doesn’t establish that you’ve found those computations. There are lots of ways to split a matrix into redundant pieces. The interesting question is what constraints or training objective make the pieces correspond to something the network actually uses, rather than just an arbitrary way of rewriting the same matrix.

r001.rationale: The response says overlapping rank-one terms can sum to the matrix and that sparse features can be represented without each having its own orthogonal activation direction, describing features in superposition.

r002.rationale: It describes each term as reading an input direction and writing an output direction, but does not clearly identify the terms as individual computations or parts of computations the network performs.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention stochastic estimation or causal importance for determining which components matter for an input.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, so the key distinction is between a basis and an overcomplete set of components. If you have an activation space of dimension d, you can only have d linearly independent directions. But you can have many more directions than that if you allow them to be linearly dependent.

And a rank-one component is an outer product of two vectors. You can think of it as reading along one direction in the input space and writing along another direction in the output space. A matrix can be expressed as a sum of lots of those. Its rank puts a limit on how many you need, but it doesn’t put a limit on how many you can use.

The catch is that once you allow an overcomplete decomposition, there are lots of different ways to do it. So reconstructing the matrix isn’t enough to tell you that you’ve found something meaningful. You need additional constraints or an objective that favors components corresponding to distinct computations—perhaps components that are used sparsely across inputs. The hope is that this lets us separate computations that share the same activation space, rather than assuming that each computation gets its own independent dimension.

r001.rationale: The response describes overcomplete, linearly dependent directions and shared activation space, but does not say that rank-one components read feature directions represented in superposition.

r002.rationale: It says the decomposition may identify components corresponding to distinct computations and explains each rank-one component as reading along an input direction and writing along an output direction.

r003.rationale: It does not mention stochastic estimation or causal importance for determining which components matter for a given input.
